name: Last Chance Diet

card.summary: A 1970s liquid protein fast promoted for rapid weight loss, and a landmark case study in the risks of very-low-calorie diets.
card.note: Linked to sudden cardiac deaths in the late 1970s; modern very-low-calorie diets are medically supervised.

quick.overview:
The Last Chance Diet was a liquid protein modified fast popularised by a 1976 book of the same name. Followers consumed a liquid protein product in place of food to lose weight quickly, aiming for a leaner look.

It became widely known after sudden deaths among dieters in 1977 to 1978. Physicians reported cardiac arrhythmias, and analyses pointed to poor-quality protein, electrolyte deficiencies and lack of medical supervision.
quick.how: Historically, dieters replaced meals with a liquid protein preparation, often collagen-derived, for extended periods. Today's comparable approach is the medically supervised very-low-calorie diet using formulated meal replacements.
quick.risks: Case reports and reviews documented arrhythmias and sudden death, with magnesium and potassium deficiencies discussed. Authorities since required warnings on very-low-calorie protein products, and guidelines limit modern versions to supervised use.

lead: The Last Chance Diet was a liquid protein modified fast promoted in a 1976 book and used by many people seeking rapid weight loss. It is a form of protein-sparing modified fast, in which protein intake is intended to limit muscle loss while energy intake is very low.[1]

Use of the diet led to serious reports. In 1978 a New England Journal of Medicine case report described sudden death in a patient on a liquid protein diet,[2] a JAMA report discussed magnesium deficiency and cardiac arrest,[3] and a 1980 report described arrhythmias.[4] An analysis of 44 publicized deaths concluded that most patients had been inappropriately managed and that no single factor explained the deaths.[5]

The episode shaped later policy: the FDA has required warnings on very-low-calorie protein products since 1984, and modern very-low-calorie diets are formulated with vitamins and minerals and used under medical supervision.[6]

chain: Rapid weight loss and a leaner appearance
angle.text: The diet was used to lose weight fast and look leaner. It is documented mainly for its harms, and later medical protocols use formulated products under supervision.

paras: The protein-sparing modified fast was described by Blackburn in the early 1970s, and the 1976 book The Last Chance Diet presented a liquid protein version.[1] A 1978 review argued that the fatal cases used hydrolysed collagen with tryptophan, which lacks other essential amino acids.[1]

In 1979, Isner and colleagues reported 17 sudden deaths among liquid protein dieters, attributed to cardiac causes with prolonged QT interval.[1] A 1981 analysis of 44 publicized deaths found that 32 of 36 analysable patients were managed inappropriately, and the four possibly proper cases all had known heart disease.[5] A study in obese rats on a commercial liquid protein product reported ECG abnormalities, and a 1983 study reported that vigorous supplementation prevented arrhythmias and mineral depletion.[7][8]

Wikipedia notes that 58 people in the US were reported to have died on liquid protein diets in 1978, that the FDA has required warnings on protein very-low-calorie products under 400 kcal since 1984, and that NICE guidelines (2014) allow such diets only under medical supervision for up to 12 weeks.[6] In a 1995 trial of 1,004 patients on a 520 kcal/day liquid protein programme, ursodeoxycholic acid was tested for preventing gallstones.[9]

Research includes the case reports and analyses above, a 1983 study of supplementation,[7] and a randomized trial of gallstone prevention during a very-low-calorie programme.[9] Modern reviews describe larger short-term weight loss with very-low-calorie diets but loss of lean mass and gallstone risk.[6]

timeline.event: Case reports of sudden death and magnesium deficiency.[2][3]
FDA begins requiring warnings on protein very-low-calorie products.[6]
